transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to investing by the books, a podcast by Red Eye.
I'm your host, Eddie Palmian, and with me here in the studio is my friend and colleague,
Niklas Savos. How are you?
I'm great and really happy to introduce today's interview,
and we are now also very close to Red Eye's annual serial acquires conference on March 6th in Stockholm.
Yes, we've been organizing this conference over the past months and it really feels like a birthday
coming up, so I know many of you listeners will join us in Stockholm and I'm really looking forward
to see you. And for today's episode of investing by the books, we have the pleasure of sharing
an exclusive conversation where Christian Billinger talks to Edward Chancellor about his book,
Capital Returns. So Niklas, for new listeners, who is Christian and why has he taken our place this time?
Christian Billinger is a London-based investor heading his family office,
Billinger for Welting, and since a number of years, Christian is a contributor to the
investing by the book's website and also this podcast. In Episode 8, he interviewed Lauren's
Cunningham about his book, Quality Investing, and in Episode 32, we had a great pleasure of
discussing Terry Smith's book, Investing for Growth, with Christian. So Eddie, who is Edward
Chancellor? Chancellor is a financial historian, a journalist and investment strategist. He is
currently a columnist for Reuters breaking news, and an occasional contributor to, for example,
Wall Street Journal and Financial Times. Edward Chancellor is also a prominent author,
with titles including Devil Take the Hindmost, Capital Account, and The Price of Time.
And for this episode, the focus will be on his book, Capital Returns. So what is this one about?
Capital Returns is a book that details Marathon asset management's equity investing strategy,
and specifically, it also covers the years after the IT crisis in 2000. And Marathon was founded in 1986,
and is a privately owned investment management firm based in London, which has produced several
iconic investors, such as Nick Sleep and Jeremy Hosking. A highlight for me with the book is Marathon's
deep focus on the supply side dynamics of businesses where large capital investments in a sector
typically leads to low returns ahead. Capital Returns was published in 2015 by Paul Grave MacMillum,
and we are honored to have its author on the show today. Here comes Christian Bill English
Conversation with Edward Chancellor.
Just in a few brief sentences, how did the whole project come about, what was your relationship
to the guys of Marathon? Why did you decide to pursue this at the time? I know you'd been involved
in the capsule accounts book, right? But how did the whole thing come about?
Capital return was the first book I edited on the capital cycle, and that,
how did that come about? That came back because Marathon had been taking a big bet against the
tech bubble back in 1999, 2000. The biggest risk you were taking from an investment perspective
was whether to be underweight, T-Mobile, or Nokia, or any of these other TMT companies.
So Marathon had, and I just written this book on
financial history, a financial speculation called Devoteye Mist. So in 1999, 2000, all the bearish
investors were quite keen on Devoteye Mist because it gave us historical support for their position.
But what was interesting about the Marathon approach is that as you know, it's entirely
focused on the supply side, and one of the things I noted about
speculative manias is in most cases, not always, but in most cases, they engender a massive increase
in supply, and it's that increase in supply from a surge of investment that actually plays
a major role in the poor returns that the investments produce. One example is the
British railway mania of the 1840s, which is a nice case because railways at the time were
new technology, and the early railways were highly profitable, and then there was a railway mania
and a surge of investment in railways, and the surge of investment in railways was such that
roughly the amount of new investment was estimated roughly equivalent to English, British GDP at
the time, or another way of looking at it is the new railways proposed were equivalent to the
entire existing toll-pike systems, the systems of roads in the country, and as the upshot of that,
the investment was indiscriminate, and so I like to cite the case of three different
railway lines running between London and Petersburg. So massive over-investment, and that massive
over-investment meant that once mania had got passed, the railway system was locked into
permanently lower returns. Now, if you then fast forward to the 1990s, we then got a surge of
investment, particularly in telecoms. I mean, leaving aside, obviously, you've got a lot of
investment in relatively small miscellaneous.coms, but the real investment was laying out the telecoms
infrastructure for the internet, and what was interesting about that case was that there was one
predominant forecast for growth of internet traffic. The internet traffic was said to be doubling
every two months, and in fact, actually, it turns out, we knew this at the time because some
academic University of Minnesota had actually crunched the numbers, that actually the data,
the data traffic was any grain doubling every four months, so a huge amount of huge discrepancy
in the forecast and massive investment, you see, and it set this combination of an inaccurate
demand forecast with a surge in supply that brings about the lower returns. Anyhow, so that was how
and the capital account book, you know, look, really was looking through the sort of
wreckage of the TMT bubble from an investment perspective. And then, and actually, I got the job
because I'd been at Lazards a few years earlier with a colleague who then went to a
called Charles Carter, who then went to work for Marathons. It was Charles who ought me into the
project. So one of the things that sort of strikes me about the idea of capital
cycle investing is that I think the first time I read the book, or certainly when I first heard of
the concept, I think I assume, like many people, that it's all about investing counter-cyclically
or identifying, you know, flows of capital into and out of industries, and that that seems to be
one important part of it. But it seems like there's a second important part, which I think
became more important over time to Marathons, which is to invest in companies that all together
avoid the impact of that capital cycle. Is that a fair reading of the book?
People sometimes say, what does this capital cycle theory only apply to capital intensive
industries like mining? And it works for energy extraction, it works for sending conductors.
But I think really, as a discipline, you can use it for just by every investment because either
you are in the capital cycle, and going through the vicissitudes, the capital cycle, the sort of
over-investment, and under-investment, in which case you need to time your entrance and exit
from an investment, or you're in a business that is exempt from the capital cycle. And the classic
case would be a so-called quality company, a quality monopolistic business. But then I think
Marathons sort of took it into the area of what you might call quality cyclicals of quality
industries. And particularly into, as you know, the global supply chains, you have relatively small
companies that have niches within a global supply chain. And that niche makes them relatively secure.
It doesn't mean that they won't suffer a loss of a contraction when the economy turns
down, but on the whole, they're much safer from the surge in over-investment. So you should
always think of the capital cycle when making any investment really, even if it's only to say
actually the capital cycle doesn't really apply in this instance.
So one of the interesting things I find about what you said there is that most investors seem to,
although I also think these labels are misleading value and growth or value and quality, but
most investors, I think, you know, define themselves and other people define them quite clearly as
either a traditional value, or as quality, or as growth, but it seems that this approach would
enable you, and actually in the case of math, and they were able to implement both. So in the case
of companies where the capital cycle does apply, that would be more similar to a traditional or
deep value investor, and where it doesn't apply, you'd probably typically define that more as a
quality or a growth investor. I mean, is it fair to say that it couldn't cover that whole spectrum
of styles or philosophies? Well, if you think of a value and a growth, you know, the value strategy
and the growth strategy, value is in, you know, truly defined as businesses selling below its
book value. If you're in an industry where the businesses are selling below their book,
there is on the whole, not 100%, but in those, there's a disincentive to invest, yeah, and so
and then take growth, creating above your book, there is an incentive to invest. So in fact, growth
and value are, have an underlying capital cycle impetus to them, and I don't think this is really
being, I don't think this has really been teased out when the growth and value were sort of identified
as value, value was identified as something that was expected to act before the growth to
under the form in the, in the, in the long distant days. So and then I think, you know, you think
of it now, a new factor has been added to, or two new factors really, from French and farmer,
you know, develop these models of different factors leading to superior returns. One is straightforward
the investment, and that was sort of interesting because they came out with that in 2015, so
good 10 years after capital accounts been published. And quality, and quality as I go back to what
I was saying earlier is that if you're in a monopolistic position, you're not going to be,
you're not going to have to invest, you know, along with, with, with your competitors,
say, you're, you're getting everything else being equal, you'll have a more disciplined
approach to investing because you're in a stronger competitive position. So that seems to be one
reason why quality is a better, you know, to the extent we want to use labels at all, but, but
label for those companies that sort of almost sit outside the capital cycle as opposed to growth,
because of course, as you say in the book, growth event, anything, certainly when it comes to
asset growth is, if anything, is sort of the contraindicator, right? But, but often causes
the issues that you could experience with the cycle. So quality, quality is in interesting and
that it has delivered positive alpha. I think since time immemorial, and this is, I'm citing
my, my old boss at GMO, Jeremy Grant, who developed quality strategy at GMO, he says
quality can be expected to add 100 base points a year of performance readiness to the market,
even though by definition quality is less risky than the market. So it has, it has a lower
beta than the market, but it has a higher return. I think probably underlying it are these, you know,
what Warren Buffett called Modes, and those Modes are, as I say, protecting you from the vicissitudes
of over investment. But then to go back to growth, you can have a business that is, so to speak,
growth stock, you know, trading above book, growing fast, and then the question is, is it caught
up in a negative capital cycle or is it a benign one? And if it's a benign one, you, you can expect
the higher returns to persist for longer. And likewise, frankly, you can be a value stock,
and continue to over invest and therefore expect lower returns. So one has to sort of
analyze these matters on a case by case basis. Yeah. And the progression that seems to
occurred that marathon in terms of moving increasingly towards the type of companies that
sort of almost sit outside the whole framework of the capital cycle certainly doesn't apply
in terms of the depressing returns. Do you think that was that a function of the environments,
or do you think that was an evolution of their thinking, that their approach evolved, or was it simply
a case of, you know, the sort of structural decline in bond rates, et cetera, just made for a much
more, but, you know, that made the quality sort of part of the market much more attractive.
I would say, well, go back to the value growth dichotomy. I think value, you know,
made most of that in marathon, most of the methods would have seen themselves as value shops.
But then, as I say, once you put the sort of capital cycle goggles on, you can buy both
growth and value and quality, and I don't know exactly what led to a shift in their style,
or portfolio composition, if you would call it that, because they would say their style remains
consistent. But it was very fortunate, because as you know, so roughly at the turn of the century,
the crude measures of value that have seen very reliable for previous decades,
ceased to function. So it was a nice fortuitous shift. And again, as I say, what was good about
the capital cycle, is it allows the investor to, well, it really increases the number of stocks
that an investor will consider for purchase. It does seem, you know, if you take the, if you're a
value short, and you can only buy value stocks, you're necessarily limiting the amount of potential
investments, and as you're probably aware, given the roughly 50% of value stocks, actually turn
active value traps and lose money, you're limiting your investments, and increasing your
chance of making mistakes. I don't think particularly wise. Yeah, agreed. Does this framework
apply as well to the overall market as it does to individual industries and companies? I'm asking
because some of the case studies, as I call them in chapters four to seven. So I think you
discussed some indicators that could suggest there's a bubble forming in the market, you know, or
rather the authors of the articles discussing such as speculative behavior, you know, very high
levels of IPOs, private XE transactions, etc. So do you think it's as reliable when it comes to
looking at the overall market, or is it more useful as a framework for security selection,
so to speak? I think it's an important and interesting fact to consider when you're looking
at the overall market. I mean, two things, if you have a market that declines from, from the
high level, in part, just it might be driven by valuation, the valuation might, it can be
sufficient for in down market, but it's valuation with excess supply and it seems to be key. And
I mean, take, for instance, real estate markets around the world, you know, go back to the global
financial crisis and run up to that. In the countries that had real estate bubbles and massive
increase in supply, namely United States, Ireland, and Spain, those countries suffered
very severe real estate bars, and in countries where new supply was limiting
and a residential building was limited, such as Britain and Australia. They were largely avoided
the past. Now, you know, I was interested 13 years ago, or sort of meet it after miles of the
financial crisis in what was going on in China. Chinese were investing over 50% of GDP,
and the stock market wasn't particularly valued, wasn't particularly expensive on a P basis,
it was trading at sort of 10 times earnings, and if you go and look at the returns of Chinese
equities over the last 13, 14 years, they're flat. And I think that the, I think that the low
returns from China over that period of function of massiveness allocation of capital.
Then if you, and actually go back a bit earlier to the 1990s, capital cycle was actually developed
by a former, one of the founders of marathon, Jeremy Hosking. When he was, he covered
among other things, so Asian markets for marathon. And so in the first half of 1990s, he observed
massive increase in investment in Thailand, and where you had a real estate, bubble, and
massive in search of investment. And if you look at the ratio of, well, first of all, you can see
the investment share of GDP in China, sorry, in Thailand and the other so-called tiger economies,
you can see that that, I mean, lower than China in the last decade, but sort of roughly in
the range of 40% of GDP. But actually, I actually got the numbers for the cap extra depreciation ratio
of the Thai stock market in that period. You see a very high cap extra depreciation ratio
in the mid-1990s. And it's really only when the capex collapses after the Asian crisis,
that the market is put on a firm basis for a very good recovery. I really see,
if I'm thinking about a market that is going to be in a robust state position to take off
after being depressed, you want it to be cheap, obviously. You want it to be in a benign capital
cycle, in other words, you want them to slash capital spending, which everything else being
cool will lead to higher profit margins going forward. And you probably want to be in as a benign
face in the credit cycle. And if you have all those stars aligned, then things will probably
go well. But I certainly feel that valuation alone is not the answer.
I mean, say, take, for instance, the US stock market in the last decade. So by sort of,
you know, the markets recovered after GFC pretty quickly. And I was working at GMO,
you know, we used some mean-reverting valuation models for the entire market. And the US market
looked expensive on a valuation basis. However, for a variety of reasons, American companies weren't
investing very much, as you're probably aware. So you could say high valuation and a depressed capital
cycle that meant that the US carried on introducing superb investment returns over the last decade,
where it goes to China, low valuations and high investment and miserable returns. You know, you
mentioned the TMT bubble in the 1990s. You can see, you see the valuation market going up on a sort
of, you know, you could look at it on a sort of tokens queue basis with placement costs basis.
And then if you, I don't know if I have it in the book, but I do chart investment GDP against the
tokens queue and you can see it coming up. So, you know, these things don't always hold. You can
have a highly valued market that doesn't elicit a lot of investment. And then you can have one
that does. So again, you just have to see what's going on. Yeah, they're very, they're two very
interesting case studies that once you mention the US and China, would math and use the framework?
I, I don't think, I think they use it on the stock. I have asked whether they, whether they
use it for sort of allocating between markets. And I don't think they do which, you know, which
is their choice. No, of course. And not in terms of balance sheet management, either in your
impression as in, you know, increasing or decreasing cash levels or employing leverage or
would they, do you know whether they would typically use the framework for that or not really.
When you see increasing leverage, what do you mean by that? Well, either either taking on leverage
or increasing cash levels in the portfolio as in keeping some liquidity dry. Yeah, I, I didn't think
they would, why they wouldn't use leverage. I would have thought their mandates to be fully
invested. So, but you, do you think it could be used for that safer, you know, a private investor
who wants to adopt the framework? Do you think it can sort of helpfully be used for managing
cash levels, et cetera? It certainly depends because assuming that you're an international investor,
you're likely to find, it's very rare that you're going to find the whole world caught up in
a sort of investment frenzy. I mean, it's not, you know, in the late 90s that pretty much was
case. Do you think it works as well? The framework when it comes to capital light industry. So,
if you look at software, for instance, where it's more difficult, at least, to use the same kind
of metrics that you would for, say, traditional industry, right? In terms of Catholics to depreciation
and some of the other, or, you know, you could look at long growth for a bank, but for some of these,
say, software and other digitally enabled companies. Do you think the framework, it may work as
well in principle, but how can you apply it as easily to those types of businesses? I mean,
the problem with tech companies is they tend to expand their investment. And you're, as you're
probably aware, some analysts will actually adjust that so you can see what their actual investment
has been, but you need to look where we are at the moment. You've got, you know, frenzy of investment
in AI at the moment. And, you know, that AI investment, undergoing at the moment is sort of
roughly on par and aggregate with the mining CapEx boom of early 2010s. So, that's quite a lot
of CapEx. And, you know, frankly, everything else being equal, we would expect that to deliver some
hefty disappointments at some stage in the future. Say, yeah, you have to, you have to play
with the numbers, but, you know, you can do it. I mean, all the value guys now make an adjustment
software by turning their expenses into investment. I did want to ask you about what you just touched
upon because the book, I think, extends the articles in their extend to 2015, right? So, I wanted to
ask you about whether you have any examples developing since then a clear, obvious sort of excesses
in the market, you know, given so we're recording this in December 23. But you mentioned AI
potentially. You look at other things like, you know, China, I guess, has been a more sort of long,
long-running story. But, if you look at, you know, electric vehicles or any other examples,
are there any obvious places to be looking? Do you think at the moment where there seems to be
hysteria and too much capital going in? And, well, I mean, I think the EV is a, you know,
a good case. And when I talk on the capital cycle, in recent years, I have been underlining the EV
investment search. And as you saw, that was also accompanied by, you
know, search of new papers. So, there's a lot of those SPACs, you know, launched in 2020 were
EV related. And yeah, I think that'll do the car makers really. I wouldn't touch them.
Are there any other ones? Any other obvious case studies at the moment?
You know, what I find quite interesting is the inverse. You know, obviously, what one's looking
out from an investment perspective, not over-investment, but under-investment. And it strikes me
to be massive under-investment in energy. And if you're back in 2020, market cap of Tesla
exceeded all entire US energy industry, you know, the exons of the chevrons of this world.
And the very depressed investment in oil, you know, there was all this talker oil investments
being stranded assets. Again, this is an absolutely classic capital cycle era where you
looking at a sort of long-term projection forecast. You're ignoring the fact that actually
demand for oil just trenches up. You know, it goes up every year regardless of how many
cop conferences they hold. And they cut investment. And I heard, for instance, I, you know,
I was at a conference last year and a guy presented it. What I thought was a classic capital cycle
case where the entire offshore US drilling industry went bust in 2020. And the person who
personally was presenting this idea, he was targeting a stock called Noble. As he's
these ships, very positioned ships with drilling in deep water. Those ships were made in
Singapore and in Scandinavia. And this guy went to the shipbuilders and the shipbuilders said,
we're not making this anymore. We're not making these boats anymore. So you've got a demand
for oil going on. And a very severe capital constraint, at least in the
herb deep sea oil drilling. And you know, this guy bought the stock at seven. I think he was
targeting it last year in last October, 35, not roughly 50. It struck me as being a very nice idea.
That fitted with my view that there was massive underinvestment in energy going forward. And as
you see, you name the last couple of years, US energy companies have done very nicely.
On the positive side, you know, the miners look relatively sort of, you know, they've been,
you know, they had their bus in 2014. And they haven't really picked up investment since then.
And although I understand, you know, a man has been following it very closely that,
you know, the sort of sub segment of Lithium, which has been crashing this year. And I think
I think that Lithium did have a sort of massive surge of investment. So they got locked into a
negative capital cycle, but broadly speaking, the miners seem to be in a relatively benign place in
the capital cycle. I mean, do you have any other cases that you that come to mind for?
Well, one of the follow ups I wanted to ask you also around the others,
where we've seen the excess investment going in. So take EVs or I guess it's always difficult to
know until much later. It does feel like some of the many of these sort of excesses haven't been
cleared out fully or meaningfully. Is that a fair point? Do you agree with that?
What do you disagree? Do you feel that they have largely been sort of cleared?
You have to distinguish in private equity and bench capital. Private equity on the whole
doesn't need to an increase in capital investment. It tries to
sweat its assets. Whereas there's been this tremendous VC boom, if the last 13 years will say,
I did look at the numbers a while back. And in terms of the amount of money flowing into VC,
it was a record at record levels. These VC funds, they're not listed, but they have
they do trade. And what I understand is that they are trading a massive discount to their
appraised value. So if you want to buy into a VC fund, you can get it for some understand,
provides you 30% less than its praise value. Those funds also, they make capital calls
in future. So you don't just put the money out, but you commit yourself to providing more capital
in future. And the problem with that, when people are in bubble mode, is that they see a run of
decent returns and they assume money is going to be there. They get a bit overconfident. And then
when the time comes that they don't have money, and then they have to fire sell assets. So
so I would I suspect under the surface things are not very good in that space. And that they probably
probably will get worse in the next year or so. I imagine.
And when it comes to public markets, when you look at the broad indices, of course,
things look quite denying or even very constructive. But of course, I guess that's largely driven
by the fact that you've had this very narrow leadership. So the internals, I guess as many people
are arguing these days, are much more, have been much more difficult. Over the last 12,
24 months or so as an outside of that very narrow leadership, there's been a lot of pain.
Do you feel that on the whole? So how do we how should I think about that from a sort of capital
cycle framework? Many of these, we had that very long bull run. We had that speculative sort of
hysteria during the pandemic and I think coming out of the pandemic. And then it feels like, unlike
the the P side just referred to from November 2008, it feels like few little of that. There's
certainly at the sort of broad market level. The excess has haven't really been cleared out.
Does that make sense? Or do you feel that it's more meaningful to look at the internals and the
fact that for many companies and industries, there has been reckoning? As you said, America,
the market is kept up by the so-called magnificent seven and rest marketer. I understand it's
pretty much flat. I mean, it's very rare for a great blue market to come to an end and then
immediately a new sort of tech bubble to form. I've never seen that before. I mean, as you probably
know, I've written this book that came out last year on the history of interest for price of
time. The second part of that book is really to do with the problems that the low interest rates
have caused in various parts of the financial system. And I suppose my default position,
you know, I may be wrong, but my default position is that coming off these very low interest rates
was going to be a remarkably painful experience. And I would have thought that that's my position.
It's not really to do with capital cycles such as more to do with high valuations, misallocation
of capital. I mean, you think of all these zombies. These zombie companies are not high investment
computers. Some of them might be, but they're just companies that sort of hang on in there
when interest rates were very low. And then you know, you know, certain, you know, and the
huge amount of leverage that built up in the system when people were borrowing on very low rates.
That takes a while to work its way through the system. I would have thought in the next two or
three years that that will continue. I think this year is in a way, you know, we didn't get a
recession. The markets have been very strong. There is, you know, unemployment remains low.
And in the US, the government has a sort of nose bleed fiscal deficit.
Then you've got this AI bubble. So it's a slight time out from the bear market that
started last year. But as I say, my guess is that that isn't going to hold very much longer.
But for some or many seem to argue that, you know, the so-called magnificent seven are perhaps
the kind of companies that we talked about earlier as quality as in that they would be able to
you know, that they're not even, that they're largely not subject to the forces of the capital cycle.
Yes, but I just said, I mean, as I say earlier, that they are investing vast sums in this AI
arms race. And if you think back to earlier technological breakthroughs, the first
movers didn't invariably end up winning the game. So I don't know what's going to happen with AI,
but you know, it's conceivable that that has sort of changed the economics of these tech companies.
And you know, one of the, and as you see at the moment, these companies are being
as a ramp up the AI investment, they're accruing more market cap.
